short: Puerto Rico has no dedicated AI act. Its flagship AI framework bill has stalled and its AI institute was vetoed, but narrower laws on election deepfakes, image cloning, and government AI transparency have passed, layered onto existing consumer protection, data breach, and constitutional privacy law.
title: Puerto Rico AI Laws
subtitle: No dedicated AI act, but a real and growing patchwork of narrower AI laws and existing statutes.
body_html:
Puerto Rico has no single named AI act. The Asamblea Legislativa has instead spent the 2025-2026 session passing narrower AI bills, several of which are now law, while its two broadest attempts, a government AI framework and a taxpayer-funded AI institute, have stalled or been vetoed. As a US territory, Puerto Rico is fully subject to federal AI policy and FTC enforcement, but it has no voting members of Congress shaping that federal law, and its consumer protection framework runs through the Puerto Rico Civil Code and the Department of Consumer Affairs rather than the common-law frameworks most states use.

What the legislature did

The flagship bill, P. del S. 68, would create an AI Officer and advisory committee inside PRITS, the Puerto Rico Innovation and Technology Service, but only for executive branch agencies. It passed the Senate on April 7, 2025 with just two dissenting votes and stalled in the House, where Microjuris commentary in December 2025 called it still unenacted and too narrow, since it excludes the private sector, the judiciary, and legal practice, with no civil liability rules. A companion bill, P. del S. 769, would have created an AI Development and Innovation Institute with a $10 million annual fund. It passed both chambers by wide margins across late 2025 and mid-2026, but Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez Colon vetoed it on June 3, 2026, citing fiscal concerns.

Narrower bills fared better. P. del S. 101 requires disclosure when political ads are created or substantially modified with AI, amending the Political Campaign Oversight Law and Electoral Code, and was signed as Ley 105-2026 on June 10, 2026. P. del S. 441 amended the Right to One's Own Image law to cover likenesses and voices cloned through AI, a deepfake provision, becoming Ley 163-2026 on August 3, 2026. A bill adding AI content to PRITS cybersecurity education was signed as Ley 140-2026 on July 24, 2026, and P. del S. 622, requiring agencies to disclose AI interactions and guarantee a right to a human representative, is reported signed into law too. Still pending are P. del S. 1385, on disclosure of AI-generated synthetic spokespeople in ads, and P. del S. 1226, which would bar insurers from denying claims through algorithms alone, backed by the Insurance Commissioner's Office over industry objection.

What already applies without a dedicated AI act

Several existing statutes already reach AI-enabled conduct. DACO's organic law (Ley Num. 5 of 1973) covers unfair and deceptive practices and applies to AI-driven scams with or without a new AI statute. Ley 111-2005, Puerto Rico's data breach notification law, applies whether or not AI caused the exposure. Ley 39-2012 requires businesses to post privacy notices for personal information collected online, and Ley 38-2016 restricts commercial collection of consumer data at the point of a transaction. The Right to One's Own Image law, amended by Ley 163-2026, gives Puerto Ricans a direct claim against AI-cloned likenesses and voices. Beneath it all sits Article II, Section 8 of the Puerto Rico Constitution, guaranteeing protection against abusive attacks on honor, reputation, and private or family life, a right Puerto Rico courts read broadly. Federal law layers on top: the FTC Act's ban on unfair and deceptive practices applies exactly as in the fifty states, and federal AI executive orders bind Puerto Rico agencies too, even though the territory has no vote in Congress to help write that law.

What the Department of Justice has done

Puerto Rico's Departamento de Justicia has not issued formal AI enforcement guidance, an AI-specific legal opinion, or a public AI enforcement action as of this writing. Its main documented AI activity was educational, not regulatory: at the 32nd Annual Conference of the Public Ministry, Attorneys, and Property Registrars in June 2024, prosecutors and government attorneys held training sessions on AI's effect on legal practice, and panelists noted the Puerto Rico Supreme Court was separately reviewing its ethics rules for AI use by lawyers. The more active consumer-facing responder has actually been DACO. In May 2026, DACO publicly warned about a deepfake video using AI-generated voice and face recreation of Puerto Rico's Secretary of State to promote a fraudulent investment scheme.

What this means

Puerto Rico is not an ungoverned space for AI, but it is a fragmented one. Its comprehensive government AI framework has stalled in the House, and its AI development institute was vetoed for cost reasons, so there is still no single law setting baseline rules for AI the way Colorado, Texas, or Utah have done. What exists instead is a set of topic-specific laws, on election deepfakes, image cloning, and cybersecurity curricula, layered onto general consumer protection, data breach, and constitutional privacy law that already reaches much AI-enabled harm. DACO, not the Department of Justice, is functioning as Puerto Rico's practical first responder to AI fraud. Because Puerto Rico is a territory rather than a state, its residents get the same federal AI enforcement floor as everyone else, without a vote in setting it.
